meta.subject: Geography
meta.title: Drainage
meta.intro: The drainage systems of India, Himalayan and Peninsular rivers, river basins, lakes, inland drainage and the need for water and river conservation.

objectives: Explain drainage using geographical concepts and Indian examples.
Identify the important terms, patterns, processes and locations in this chapter.
Interpret maps, tables and geographical evidence.
Connect the chapter with human life, environment and regional development.

blocks.text: Drainage describes the river system of an area. A river and its tributaries form a drainage system, while the area drained by a river and its tributaries is called a drainage basin.
The area from which a river and its tributaries collect surface runoff.
An elevated ridge or upland that separates two drainage basins. The Ambala region is an important water divide between the Indus and Ganga systems.
The drainage pattern depends on slope, geological structure, rock resistance, climate and the history of landform development.

blocks.title: Common drainage patterns
blocks.text: Dendritic drainage resembles tree branches; trellis drainage develops where hard and soft rocks occur in parallel bands; radial drainage flows outward from a central highland.
The Himalayan river systems are generally perennial because they receive water from both rainfall and melting snow and glaciers. Their long courses cross mountains, plains and deltas.
The Indus rises near Lake Mansarovar in the Tibetan region and flows through Ladakh before entering Pakistan. Its major tributaries include the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej.
The Ganga system begins with the headstreams Bhagirathi and Alaknanda, which meet at Devprayag. The river is joined by major tributaries such as the Yamuna, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi and Son.
The Brahmaputra rises in Tibet, where it is known as the Tsangpo. It enters Arunachal Pradesh as the Siang/Dihang and flows through Assam before entering Bangladesh.

blocks.title: River behaviour
blocks.text: Himalayan rivers carry large sediment loads, create extensive floodplains and often change course in their lower reaches.
Most Peninsular rivers depend mainly on monsoon rainfall. Their courses are generally shorter and more fixed than those of Himalayan rivers because they flow across an older and more stable plateau.
The Narmada and Tapi flow westwards through rift valleys and enter the Arabian Sea through estuaries. The Godavari is the largest Peninsular river basin and is often called the Dakshin Ganga.
The Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri flow eastwards and form deltas before entering the Bay of Bengal. Their water is important for irrigation, drinking supply, industry and hydroelectricity.
Lakes may be formed by tectonic movements, glaciers, river action, coastal processes or human activity. Some are freshwater lakes, while others are saline or brackish.

Wular in Jammu and Kashmir is a major freshwater lake. Dal is also located in Kashmir. Sambhar in Rajasthan is a salt lake. Chilika in Odisha is a brackish-water lagoon, and Pulicat lies along the Andhra Pradesh–Tamil Nadu coast.
Lakes regulate river flow, store water, support fisheries and tourism, recharge groundwater and provide habitats for birds and aquatic life.

blocks.title: Chilika Lake
blocks.text: Chilika is a large brackish lagoon on the Odisha coast. It supports fisheries, migratory birds and local livelihoods, making wetland conservation important.
Rivers are stressed by untreated sewage, industrial effluents, agricultural runoff, solid waste, excessive water withdrawal and encroachment on floodplains.

Pollution reduces dissolved oxygen, harms aquatic organisms and affects drinking water, irrigation, fisheries and public health. Dams and barrages can alter sediment movement and river ecology, so planning must consider both benefits and impacts.
River conservation requires sewage treatment, industrial compliance, efficient irrigation, protection of wetlands and floodplains, environmental flows, community participation and monitoring.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: A river is not only a channel carrying water; it is an interconnected ecosystem supporting people, agriculture, biodiversity and landscapes.
